reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Situs inversus totalis denotes complete mirror-image reversal of both thoracic and abdominal viscera, with cardiac apex, aortic arch, stomach and spleen on the right and liver on the left.

In contrast to heterotaxy, situs inversus totalis carries a relatively low incidence of major congenital heart disease, most affected individuals having structurally normal hearts in mirror-image configuration.

Roughly a quarter of individuals with situs inversus totalis have primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome), so persistent sinopulmonary disease, chronic otitis and subfertility should prompt ciliary evaluation.
Congenitally corrected transposition and other conotruncal lesions occur more often in situs inversus than in the general population and warrant careful segmental echocardiographic assessment.
Atypical presentation of common disease is the rule: left-sided appendicitis, left-sided biliary colic and a right-sided cardiac apex on examination are classic traps.
Standard ECG electrode placement produces a spurious picture (inverted P in lead I, reversed praecordial progression); mirror-image lead placement restores a normal-appearing trace.
A segmental (sequential) approach naming atrial situs, ventricular loop and great-artery relationship is essential before any surgical or catheter intervention.
Interventional and surgical teams must anticipate reversed anatomy for central venous access, coronary angiography, and abdominal surgery to avoid wrong-side procedures.
reference.pathophysiology: Situs inversus arises from disruption of the normal left-right axis patterning established during early embryogenesis at the primitive node, where motile monocilia generate a leftward extra-embryonic fluid flow (nodal flow) that biases asymmetric expression of the Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 signalling cascade. When this laterality signal is randomised or reversed, the viscera and cardiac tube loop in mirror-image fashion, producing complete reversal (situs inversus totalis) when the process is coordinated across all organ fields. In primary ciliary dyskinesia the nodal cilia are immotile or dyskinetic, so laterality is determined at random, explaining why about half of affected individuals have situs inversus and half situs solitus. Because the reversal is usually symmetric and complete, atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial concordance is preserved in mirror image and the heart is typically structurally normal, distinguishing this condition from the abnormal midline symmetry of heterotaxy.
additionalDifferentials: dextroposition from pulmonary hypoplasia or diaphragmatic hernia
congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries
primary ciliary dyskinesia without laterality defect
acquired mediastinal shift mimicking cardiac malposition
additionalInvestigations: transthoracic echocardiography with formal segmental analysis
abdominal ultrasound documenting hepatic, splenic and gastric position
chest radiograph noting cardiac apex, gastric bubble and aortic arch side
ECG with both standard and mirror-image lead placement
nasal nitric oxide measurement and ciliary studies where primary ciliary dyskinesia is suspected
cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for detailed situs and vascular mapping before intervention
genetic testing for ciliopathy and laterality genes in selected cases
redFlags: chronic productive cough, recurrent sinusitis or bronchiectasis suggesting primary ciliary dyskinesia
cyanosis, murmur or failure to thrive indicating associated structural heart disease
atypical or contralateral pain suggesting missed left-sided appendicitis or biliary disease
unexplained subfertility in the context of a laterality defect
planned surgery or intervention where reversed anatomy risks a wrong-side procedure
reference.prognosis: Isolated situs inversus totalis with a structurally normal heart is compatible with a normal lifespan and requires mainly awareness for atypical disease presentation. Prognosis is chiefly determined by any coexisting congenital heart disease or by the respiratory and fertility consequences of associated primary ciliary dyskinesia.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal heart and omitting a full segmental echocardiographic assessment.
Misinterpreting the ECG as ischaemic or abnormal when electrodes are placed conventionally.
Overlooking primary ciliary dyskinesia in a patient presenting only with situs inversus.
Diagnosing situs inversus when the true picture is heterotaxy, thereby underestimating cardiac and splenic risk.
Failing to communicate reversed anatomy to surgical, anaesthetic and interventional teams.

European Respiratory Society guidelines on primary ciliary dyskinesia
management: Perform segmental echocardiographic assessment and refer to cardiology to identify and manage any associated congenital heart defects such as congenitally corrected transposition or conotruncal lesions

Screen for primary ciliary dyskinesia with nasal nitric oxide and ciliary studies where sinopulmonary disease, chronic otitis or subfertility coexist, instituting airway clearance and prompt antibiotics for infections if confirmed
Document the mirror-image anatomy prominently to avoid diagnostic traps such as left-sided appendicitis or right-sided biliary colic and to guide safe surgery
Use mirror-image ECG lead placement and annotate all imaging with the situs to prevent misinterpretation
Manage the respiratory and fertility consequences of associated ciliary disease with respiratory physiotherapy and fertility referral
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across cardiology, respiratory, ENT and surgery, flagging reversed anatomy before any operative or interventional procedure
